claim: PML NBs are nuclear membrane-less organelles physically associated with chromatin.
source: Promyelocytic leukemia Nuclear Bodies (PML NBs) are nuclear membrane-less organelles physically associated with chromatin underscoring their crucial role in genome function.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract as a characterization of PML NBs.

claim: The H3.3 histone chaperone complex HIRA accumulates in PML NBs upon senescence.
source: The H3.3 histone chaperone complex HIRA accumulates in PML NBs upon senescence, viral infection or IFN-I treatment in primary cells.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by citations in the introduction (Banumathy et al., 2009; Jiang et al., 2011; Rai et al., 2011; Zhang et al., 2005).

claim: The H3.3 histone chaperone complex HIRA accumulates in PML NBs upon viral infection.
source: The H3.3 histone chaperone complex HIRA accumulates in PML NBs upon senescence, viral infection or IFN-I treatment in primary cells.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by citations (Cohen et al., 2018; McFarlane et al., 2019; Rai et al., 2017).

claim: The H3.3 histone chaperone complex HIRA accumulates in PML NBs upon IFN-I treatment in primary cells.
source: The H3.3 histone chaperone complex HIRA accumulates in PML NBs upon senescence, viral infection or IFN-I treatment in primary cells.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1 and Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Intermolecular SUMO-SIM interactions are an essential mechanism for HIRA recruitment in PML NBs.
source: By using specific approaches, we identify intermolecular SUMO-SIM interactions as an essential mechanism for HIRA recruitment in PML NBs.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data in Figures 2 and 3, including PLA assays, SUMO depletion experiments, and Affimer experiments.

claim: PML NBs function as nuclear depot centers to regulate HIRA distribution in the nucleus.
source: Hence, we describe a role of PML NBs as nuclear depot centers to regulate HIRA distribution in the nucleus, dependent both on SP100 and DAXX/H3.3 levels.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by data in Figure 4 showing that HIRA nucleoplasmic levels decrease upon IFNβ treatment and that DAXX and H3.3 levels modulate HIRA accumulation in PML NBs.

claim: HIRA distribution in the nucleus is dependent on SP100 levels.
source: Hence, we describe a role of PML NBs as nuclear depot centers to regulate HIRA distribution in the nucleus, dependent both on SP100 and DAXX/H3.3 levels.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by data in Figure 3—figure supplement 2 showing that SP100 depletion abrogates HIRA partitioning in PML NBs.

claim: HIRA distribution in the nucleus is dependent on DAXX/H3.3 levels.
source: Hence, we describe a role of PML NBs as nuclear depot centers to regulate HIRA distribution in the nucleus, dependent both on SP100 and DAXX/H3.3 levels.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by data in Figure 4 showing that DAXX knockdown and H3.3 overexpression affect HIRA accumulation in PML NBs.

claim: PML is required for interferon-stimulated genes (ISGs) transcription upon IFN-I stimulation.
source: Upon IFN-I stimulation, PML is required for interferon-stimulated genes (ISGs) transcription and PML NBs become juxtaposed to ISGs loci at late time points of IFN-I treatment.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by data in Figure 5—figure supplement 1C showing that PML depletion reduces ISGs expression.

claim: PML NBs become juxtaposed to ISGs loci at late time points of IFN-I treatment.
source: Upon IFN-I stimulation, PML is required for interferon-stimulated genes (ISGs) transcription and PML NBs become juxtaposed to ISGs loci at late time points of IFN-I treatment.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by immuno-FISH data in Figure 5A-B showing decreased distance between PML NBs and ISG loci at 48 hr of IFNβ treatment.

claim: HIRA and PML are necessary for the prolonged H3.3 deposition at the transcriptional end sites of ISGs.
source: HIRA and PML are necessary for the prolonged H3.3 deposition at the transcriptional end sites of ISGs, well beyond the peak of transcription.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by ChIP-Seq data in Figure 6E-G showing reduced H3.3 at ISG TES regions upon HIRA or PML depletion.

claim: HIRA accumulation in PML NBs is dispensable for H3.3 deposition on ISGs.
source: Though, HIRA accumulation in PML NBs is dispensable for H3.3 deposition on ISGs.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by data in Figure 7A showing that SP100 depletion, which prevents HIRA accumulation in PML NBs, does not prevent H3.3 loading at ISGs.

claim: PML NBs are 0.1–1 μm diameter hollow sphere structures.
source: PML NBs are 0.1–1 μm diameter hollow sphere structures that vary in size and number depending on cell type, cell-cycle phase, or physiological state, highlighting their stress-responsive nature.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as a structural characterization of PML NBs.

claim: PML NBs vary in size and number depending on cell type, cell-cycle phase, or physiological state.
source: PML NBs are 0.1–1 μm diameter hollow sphere structures that vary in size and number depending on cell type, cell-cycle phase, or physiological state, highlighting their stress-responsive nature.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and reflects established knowledge about PML NBs.

claim: PML protein is the primary scaffold of PML NBs.
source: The tumor-suppressor PML protein is the primary scaffold of PML NBs and forms an outer shell, together with the SP100 nuclear antigen, surrounding an inner core of dozens of proteins that localize constitutively or transiently in PML NBs.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as a fundamental characteristic of PML NBs structure.

claim: PML forms an outer shell together with SP100 nuclear antigen.
source: The tumor-suppressor PML protein is the primary scaffold of PML NBs and forms an outer shell, together with the SP100 nuclear antigen, surrounding an inner core of dozens of proteins that localize constitutively or transiently in PML NBs.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction describing the structural organization of PML NBs.

claim: PML is also known as TRIM19.
source: PML (also known as TRIM19) is a member of the tripartite motif (TRIM)-containing protein superfamily characterized by a conserved N-terminal RBCC motif essential for PML polymerization.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as an alternative name for PML.

claim: PML is a member of the tripartite motif (TRIM)-containing protein superfamily.
source: PML (also known as TRIM19) is a member of the tripartite motif (TRIM)-containing protein superfamily characterized by a conserved N-terminal RBCC motif essential for PML polymerization.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as a classification of PML.

claim: PML has a conserved N-terminal RBCC motif essential for PML polymerization.
source: PML (also known as TRIM19) is a member of the tripartite motif (TRIM)-containing protein superfamily characterized by a conserved N-terminal RBCC motif essential for PML polymerization.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction describing PML structure and function.

claim: PML has three well-characterized SUMO modification sites at lysines K65, K160, and K490.
source: Several isoforms of PML exist, all containing the RBCC motif and three well-characterized small-ubiquitin-related modifier (SUMO) modification sites at lysines K65, K160, and K490 and a SUMO interacting motif (SIM) enabling its interaction with SUMOylated proteins.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and is supported by citation (Kamitani et al., 1998) in the results section.

claim: PML has a SUMO interacting motif (SIM) enabling its interaction with SUMOylated proteins.
source: Several isoforms of PML exist, all containing the RBCC motif and three well-characterized small-ubiquitin-related modifier (SUMO) modification sites at lysines K65, K160, and K490 and a SUMO interacting motif (SIM) enabling its interaction with SUMOylated proteins.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction describing PML protein features.

claim: PML NBs are enriched in the SUMO E2 conjugating enzyme UBC9.
source: PML NBs are enriched in the SUMO E2 conjugating enzyme UBC9, which mediates SUMOylation of various proteins including PML thus enforcing PML-PML interactions via intermolecular SUMO-SIM interactions.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction describing the biochemical environment of PML NBs.

claim: UBC9 mediates SUMOylation of various proteins including PML.
source: PML NBs are enriched in the SUMO E2 conjugating enzyme UBC9, which mediates SUMOylation of various proteins including PML thus enforcing PML-PML interactions via intermolecular SUMO-SIM interactions.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction describing the function of UBC9 in PML NBs.

claim: SUMOylation of PML enforces PML-PML interactions via intermolecular SUMO-SIM interactions.
source: PML NBs are enriched in the SUMO E2 conjugating enzyme UBC9, which mediates SUMOylation of various proteins including PML thus enforcing PML-PML interactions via intermolecular SUMO-SIM interactions.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction describing the mechanism of PML NB assembly.

claim: SUMOylated proteins within PML NBs can drive the multivalent recruitment of inner core protein clients through their SIM.
source: SUMOylated proteins within PML NBs can drive the multivalent recruitment of inner core protein clients through their SIM, possibly via liquid-liquid phase separation (LLPS) mechanisms (Corpet et al., 2020; Li et al., 2020; Sahin et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations.

claim: PML NBs reside in the interchromatin nuclear space.
source: Third, while PML NBs are in general devoid of DNA, except in specific cases (for review Corpet et al., 2020), they reside in the interchromatin nuclear space (Boisvert et al., 2000) and can associate with specific genomic loci thus acting as chromosomal hubs adequately regulating associated genes (Chang et al., 2013; Ching et al., 2013; Delbarre et al., 2017; Kumar et al., 2007; Kurihara et al., 2020; Shiels et al., 2001; Wang et al., 2004).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citation (Boisvert et al., 2000).

claim: PML NBs can associate with specific genomic loci thus acting as chromosomal hubs regulating associated genes.
source: Third, while PML NBs are in general devoid of DNA, except in specific cases (for review Corpet et al., 2020), they reside in the interchromatin nuclear space (Boisvert et al., 2000) and can associate with specific genomic loci thus acting as chromosomal hubs adequately regulating associated genes (Chang et al., 2013; Ching et al., 2013; Delbarre et al., 2017; Kumar et al., 2007; Kurihara et al., 2020; Shiels et al., 2001; Wang et al., 2004).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by multiple citations.

claim: H3.3 is expressed throughout the cell cycle.
source: Among histone H3 variants, H3.3 is expressed throughout the cell cycle and is incorporated onto DNA in a DNA-synthesis-independent manner by dedicated histone chaperone complexes (Martire and Banaszynski, 2020).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citation.

claim: H3.3 is incorporated onto DNA in a DNA-synthesis-independent manner by dedicated histone chaperone complexes.
source: Among histone H3 variants, H3.3 is expressed throughout the cell cycle and is incorporated onto DNA in a DNA-synthesis-independent manner by dedicated histone chaperone complexes (Martire and Banaszynski, 2020).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citation.

claim: HIRA chaperone complex is composed of HIRA, ubinuclein 1 or ubinuclein 2 (UBN1 or UBN2) and calcineurin-binding protein CABIN1.
source: Histone cell cycle regulator A (HIRA) chaperone complex, composed of HIRA, ubinuclein 1 or ubinuclein 2 (UBN1 or UBN2) and calcineurin-binding protein CABIN1, is responsible for H3.3 deposition in transcriptionally active regions including enhancers, promoters and gene bodies, as well as in nucleosome-free regions and DNA damage sites (Goldberg et al., 2010; Ray-Gallet et al., 2011; Ray-Gallet et al., 2002; Zhang et al., 2017) (for review Martire and Banaszynski, 2020; Ricketts and Marmorstein, 2017).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction describing the composition of the HIRA complex.

claim: HIRA complex is responsible for H3.3 deposition in transcriptionally active regions including enhancers, promoters and gene bodies.
source: Histone cell cycle regulator A (HIRA) chaperone complex, composed of HIRA, ubinuclein 1 or ubinuclein 2 (UBN1 or UBN2) and calcineurin-binding protein CABIN1, is responsible for H3.3 deposition in transcriptionally active regions including enhancers, promoters and gene bodies, as well as in nucleosome-free regions and DNA damage sites (Goldberg et al., 2010; Ray-Gallet et al., 2011; Ray-Gallet et al., 2002; Zhang et al., 2017) (for review Martire and Banaszynski, 2020; Ricketts and Marmorstein, 2017).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by multiple citations.

claim: HIRA complex is responsible for H3.3 deposition in nucleosome-free regions and DNA damage sites.
source: Histone cell cycle regulator A (HIRA) chaperone complex, composed of HIRA, ubinuclein 1 or ubinuclein 2 (UBN1 or UBN2) and calcineurin-binding protein CABIN1, is responsible for H3.3 deposition in transcriptionally active regions including enhancers, promoters and gene bodies, as well as in nucleosome-free regions and DNA damage sites (Goldberg et al., 2010; Ray-Gallet et al., 2011; Ray-Gallet et al., 2002; Zhang et al., 2017) (for review Martire and Banaszynski, 2020; Ricketts and Marmorstein, 2017).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations.

claim: HIRA has been shown to be involved in the transcription-mediated recycling of parental H3.3.
source: HIRA has also been recently shown to be involved in the transcription-mediated recycling of parental H3.3 by microscopy approaches (Torné et al., 2020).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citation.

claim: HIRA complex is diffusively distributed in the nuclei of proliferating somatic cells.
source: Although HIRA complex is diffusively distributed in the nuclei of proliferating somatic cells, it accumulates in PML NBs upon various stresses such as senescence entry (Banumathy et al., 2009; Jiang et al., 2011; Rai et al., 2011; Zhang et al., 2005), viral infection (Cohen et al., 2018; McFarlane et al., 2019; Rai et al., 2017), or interferon type I (IFN-I) treatment (McFarlane et al., 2019; Rai et al., 2017), which encompasses IFNα and IFNβ cytokines.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction describing the normal localization of HIRA.

claim: Treatment of BJ cells with poly(I:C) triggered a strong accumulation of HIRA in PML NBs.
source: Treatment of human primary foreskin diploid fibroblast BJ cells with the TLR3 ligand poly(I:C), a strong stimulant of the IFN-I pathway, or with the Tumor necrosis factor α (TNFα) cytokine, triggered a strong accumulation of HIRA in PML NBs (Figure 1A–B), similarly to a control IFN-I treatment (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by data shown in Figure 1A-B.

claim: Treatment of BJ cells with TNFα triggered a strong accumulation of HIRA in PML NBs.
source: Treatment of human primary foreskin diploid fibroblast BJ cells with the TLR3 ligand poly(I:C), a strong stimulant of the IFN-I pathway, or with the Tumor necrosis factor α (TNFα) cytokine, triggered a strong accumulation of HIRA in PML NBs (Figure 1A–B), similarly to a control IFN-I treatment (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by data shown in Figure 1A-B.

claim: The accumulation of HIRA in PML NBs upon poly(I:C) or TNFα treatment was abrogated by addition of ruxolitinib.
source: The accumulation was abrogated by addition of ruxolitinib, an inhibitor of the JAK-STAT pathway downstream of the IFN-I receptor, underscoring the involvement of the IFN-I signaling pathway in primary cells (Figure 1A–B and Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by data shown in Figure 1A-B.

claim: IFNβ, poly(I:C) and TNFα induced an IFN-I dependent increase of the PML and SP100 proteins and their SUMOylated forms.
source: IFNβ, poly(I:C) and TNFα induced an IFN-I dependent increase of the PML and SP100 proteins and their SUMOylated forms (Figure 1C–D), as well as their mRNA levels (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B) confirming previous data (Gao et al., 2008; Guldner et al., 1992; Stadler et al., 1995).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by western blot data in Figure 1C-D and citations.

claim: IFNβ slightly increased HIRA mRNA (1.26 fold) and protein levels (1.34 fold).
source: Of note, IFNβ slightly increased HIRA mRNA (1.26 fold) and protein levels (1.34 fold) (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by data in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Treatment with IL-6 or IL-8 did not increase PML protein levels or SUMOylation.
source: Treatment with other pro-inflammatory cytokines such as IL-6 or the IL-8 chemokine, did not increase PML protein levels or SUMOylation (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D), nor affected HIRA localization that remained pan-nuclear (Figure 1—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by data in Figure 1—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Treatment with IL-6 or IL-8 did not affect HIRA localization that remained pan-nuclear.
source: Treatment with other pro-inflammatory cytokines such as IL-6 or the IL-8 chemokine, did not increase PML protein levels or SUMOylation (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D), nor affected HIRA localization that remained pan-nuclear (Figure 1—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by microscopy data in Figure 1—figure supplement 1E.

claim: HIRA accumulation in PML NBs was not a consequence of senescence as cells treated with IFNβ continued to replicate.
source: HIRA accumulation in PML NBs was not a consequence of senescence as cells treated with IFNβ continued to replicate as shown by EdU incorporation (Figure 1—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by EdU incorporation data in Figure 1—figure supplement 1F.

claim: Interaction foci between PML and SUMO2/3 increase significantly upon IFNβ treatment.
source: Using PLA, we detected interaction foci between PML and SUMO2/3 as expected (Sahin et al., 2016), with the number of interaction foci increasing significantly upon IFNβ treatment (Figure 2A–B), which is known to stimulate PML SUMOylation (Stadler et al., 1995).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by PLA data in Figure 2A-B.

claim: A significant interaction between HIRA and PML or HIRA and SUMO2/3 can be detected in presence of IFNβ.
source: We could detect a significant interaction between these proteins in presence of IFNβ (Figure 2A–B), accordingly to the accumulation of HIRA in PML NBs.
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by PLA data in Figure 2A-B.

claim: The molecular mass of HIRA remained unchanged upon IFNβ treatment of primary cells.
source: The molecular mass of HIRA remained unchanged upon IFNβ treatment of primary cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C), as previously described (McFarlane et al., 2019), which is not in favor of post-translational modification of HIRA with SUMO groups.
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by western blot data in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C and citation.

claim: Ectopic HIRA mutated on K809 was still recruited in PML NBs similar to the wild-type protein.
source: In addition, ectopic HIRA mutated on K809, identified as a possible SUMOylated lysine in a SUMO screen (Hendriks et al., 2014; Schimmel et al., 2014), was still recruited in PML NBs similar to the wild-type protein (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A), suggesting that at least K809 SUMOylation is dispensable for HIRA recruitment in PML NBs.
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by microscopy data in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Depletion of SUMOs led to a significant decrease of HIRA accumulation in PML NBs upon IFNβ treatment.
source: Depletion of SUMOs led to a significant decrease of HIRA accumulation in PML NBs upon IFNβ treatment (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by microscopy data in Figure 2D.

claim: In absence of SUMOs, PML NBs appear as large aggregates devoid of DAXX.
source: Of note, in absence of SUMOs, PML NBs appear as large aggregates devoid of DAXX (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B), reminiscent of the alternative PML NBs structures observed during mitosis, in human embryonic stem cells or in human sensory neurons (Corpet et al., 2020).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by microscopy data in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Increasing the pool of free SUMOs by ectopic expression did not trigger HIRA accumulation in PML NBs.
source: Increasing the pool of free SUMOs by ectopic expression did not trigger HIRA accumulation in PML NBs (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C) suggesting that SUMOs need to be conjugated to specific proteins to trigger HIRA partitioning in PML NBs.
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by microscopy data in Figure 2—figure supplement 1C.

claim: S1S2D5-His Affimer expression prevented the accumulation of HIRA in PML NBs upon IFNβ treatment.
source: S1S2D5-His Affimer expression prevented the accumulation of HIRA in PML NBs upon IFNβ treatment (Figure 3C), without affecting HIRA nor PML protein levels (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by microscopy data in Figure 3C.

claim: PML SUMOylation on K65, K160, and K490 is required for HIRA recruitment in PML NBs.
source: Upon doxycyclin induction, Myc-PML WT or its mutated form were expressed at high levels in Pml-/- MEFs (Figure 3D). Despite a recurrent diminution in the amount of the ectopic PML proteins following addition of mouse IFNα, possibly because of a lower efficiency of the doxycyline induction of ectopic PML transcription in IFN-I treated cells (Figure 3D), the wild type PML rescued HIRA accumulation in ectopically formed PML NBs unlike the PML 3K, which showed no colocalization with HIRA (Figure 3E).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by microscopy data in Figure 3E showing that PML 3K mutant does not recruit HIRA.

claim: The HIRA-HA mSIM2 showed a significant decrease in its accumulation in PML NBs with or without IFNβ treatment.
source: Interestingly, the HIRA-HA mSIM2 showed a significant decrease in its accumulation in PML NBs with (Figure 3F) or without (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C) IFNβ treatment.
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by microscopy data in Figure 3F and Figure 3—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Knock-down of SP100 abrogated HIRA partitioning in PML NBs.
source: Knock-down of SP100 abrogated HIRA partitioning in PML NBs (Figure 3—figure supplement 2A–B), confirming previous data (McFarlane et al., 2019), without impacting DAXX localization at PML NBs (Figure 3—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by microscopy data in Figure 3—figure supplement 2A and citation.

claim: SP100 depletion did not impact DAXX localization at PML NBs.
source: Knock-down of SP100 abrogated HIRA partitioning in PML NBs (Figure 3—figure supplement 2A–B), confirming previous data (McFarlane et al., 2019), without impacting DAXX localization at PML NBs (Figure 3—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by microscopy data in Figure 3—figure supplement 2C.

claim: Overexpression of an ectopic EYFP-SP100 protein rescued HIRA accumulation in PML NBs.
source: Overexpression of an ectopic EYFP-SP100 protein rescued HIRA accumulation in PML NBs, as well as an ectopic EYFP-SP100 mutated on its main SUMOylation site K297R (Figure 3—figure supplement 2D–F).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by microscopy data in Figure 3—figure supplement 2D.

claim: An ectopic EYFP-SP100 mutated on its main SUMOylation site K297R rescued HIRA accumulation in PML NBs.
source: Overexpression of an ectopic EYFP-SP100 protein rescued HIRA accumulation in PML NBs, as well as an ectopic EYFP-SP100 mutated on its main SUMOylation site K297R (Figure 3—figure supplement 2D–F).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by microscopy data in Figure 3—figure supplement 2D.

claim: Ectopic expression of HIRA led to its accumulation in PML NBs without the need of IFN-I stimulation.
source: Importantly, ectopic expression of HIRA led to its accumulation in PML NBs without the need of IFN-I stimulation (Ye et al., 2007b; Figure 4A), suggesting that PML NBs could buffer an excess of HIRA proteins.
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by microscopy data in Figure 4A and citation.

claim: Nucleoplasmic levels of HIRA outside PML NBs showed a significant decrease after IFNβ treatment.
source: In addition, quantification of nucleoplasmic levels of HIRA outside PML NBs showed a significant decrease after IFNβ treatment (Figure 4B), suggesting that PML NBs could act as sequestration places for HIRA upon IFN-I, leading to its substantial depletion from the surrounding nuclear space.
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by quantification data in Figure 4B.

claim: Knockdown of DAXX led to a significant increase of the baseline amounts of cells showing HIRA accumulation in PML NBs in the absence of IFN-I treatment.
source: Knockdown of DAXX led to a significant increase of the baseline amounts of cells showing HIRA accumulation in PML NBs in the absence of IFN-I treatment (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by microscopy data in Figure 4C.

claim: Overexpression of an ectopic Myc-DAXX protein completely abrogates HIRA accumulation in PML NBs upon IFN-I treatment.
source: The reverse approach consisting in the overexpression of an ectopic Myc-DAXX protein completely abrogates HIRA accumulation in PML NBs upon IFN-I treatment (Figure 4E and Figure 4—figure supplement 1D–E).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by microscopy data in Figure 4E.

claim: Induced expression of eH3.3 impaired accumulation of HIRA in PML NBs in cells with a strong expression of eH3.3.
source: However, close examination of individual cells showed an impaired accumulation of HIRA in PML NBs in cells with a strong expression of eH3.3, unlike low eH3.3 expressing cells (Figure 4F).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by microscopy data in Figure 4F.

claim: Depletion of HIRA had no significant impact on ISGs expression at 6 and 24 hr of IFNβ stimulation.
source: Depletion of HIRA had no significant impact on ISGs expression at 6 and 24 hr of IFNβ stimulation (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B–C), consistent with previous reports (McFarlane et al., 2019; Rai et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by qPCR data in Figure 5—figure supplement 1C and citations.

claim: PML depletion led to a significant reduction in ISGs expression both at 6 and 24 hr after IFNβ stimulation.
source: In contrast, PML depletion led to a significant reduction in ISGs expression both at 6 and 24 hr after IFNβ stimulation (Figure 5—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by qPCR data in Figure 5—figure supplement 1C.

claim: A marked decrease in the mean minimal distance of PML NBs with PML and MX1 loci was scored at 48 hr of IFNβ treatment.
source: A marked decrease in the mmd of PML NBs with the three loci was scored at 48 hr, which was significant for PML and MX1 loci, reaching a calculated mmd of 0.67 µm and 0.72 µm, respectively, as compared to 1.06 µm for the GHRL locus (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by immuno-FISH quantification data in Figure 5B.

claim: IFNβ stimulation induced H3.3 incorporation most noticeably over the distal sites of the coding regions of ISGs.
source: Remarkably, IFNβ stimulation induced H3.3 incorporation most noticeably over the distal sites of the coding regions (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by ChIP-qPCR data in Figure 6A.

claim: H3.3 deposition continued to increase for an extended period of time and was even higher at 48 hr of IFNβ.
source: Importantly, H3.3 deposition continued to increase for an extended period of time and was even higher at 48 hr of IFNβ, suggesting that it could leave a long-lasting chromatin mark on ISGs (Figure 6—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by ChIP-qPCR data in Figure 6—figure supplement 1E.

claim: The levels of H3.3 significantly increased on ISGs in IFNβ-treated cells with a clear bias towards the TES regions of the genes.
source: The levels of H3.3 significantly increased on ISGs in IFNβ-treated cells with a clear bias towards the TES regions of the genes (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by ChIP-Seq data in Figure 6B.

claim: No significant difference of H3.3 enrichment could be observed across non-ISGs.
source: In contrast, no significant difference of H3.3 enrichment could be observed across the non-ISGs (Figure 6C).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by ChIP-Seq data in Figure 6C.

claim: Knock-down of HIRA or PML led to a modest but consistent decrease in H3.3 at mid or TES regions of selected ISGs.
source: Knock-down of HIRA or PML led to a modest but consistent decrease in H3.3 at mid or TES regions of selected ISGs, suggesting the implication of these two proteins for the long-lasting H3.3 deposition on ISGs (Figure 6E, right).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by ChIP-qPCR data in Figure 6E.

claim: ChIP-Seq analysis confirmed a mild, but still significant, decrease in the loading of H3.3 at the TES on the panel of ISGs upon HIRA or PML knockdown.
source: ChIP-Seq analysis confirmed a mild, but still significant, decrease in the loading of H3.3 at the TES on the panel of ISGs (P-value = 4,76e-03 for HIRA knock-down (KD) or 1.262e-03 for PML KD, as assessed by a paired Student's t-test) (Figure 6F–G).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by ChIP-Seq data in Figure 6F-G.

claim: Overexpression of HIRA triggered an increase in H3.3 loading upon IFN-I, as compared to cells with endogenous levels of HIRA.
source: Of note, overexpression of HIRA, which increases the nucleoplasmic pool of HIRA as well as its accumulation in PML NBs (Figure 4A), triggered an increase in H3.3 loading upon IFN-I, as compared to cells with endogenous levels of HIRA (Figure 6—figure supplement 2A–B).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by ChIP-qPCR data in Figure 6—figure supplement 2A.

claim: SP100 depletion did not prevent H3.3 loading at the ISGs TES upon IFN-β stimulation, but on the contrary increased it.
source: SP100 depletion did not prevent H3.3 loading at the ISGs TES upon IFN-β stimulation, but on the contrary increased it (Figure 7A–B).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by ChIP-qPCR data in Figure 7A.

claim: SP100 depletion led to an important increase in ISGs transcription.
source: Of note, SP100 depletion led to an important increase in ISGs transcription (Figure 7—figure supplement 1B–C).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by qPCR data in Figure 7—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Simultaneous knock-down of SP100 and HIRA in IFN-I treated cells reduced H3.3 deposition at the level of the control siRNA.
source: Simultaneous knock-down of SP100 and HIRA in IFN-I treated cells (Figure 7B) reduced H3.3 deposition at the level of the control siRNA (Figure 7A).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by ChIP-qPCR data in Figure 7A.

claim: The increase in H3.3 loading on ISGs TES upon SP100 knockdown and following IFN-β stimulation is mediated by HIRA independently of its localization in PML NBs.
source: Thus, this demonstrates that the increase in H3.3 loading on ISGs TES upon SP100 knockdown and following IFN-β stimulation is mediated by HIRA independently of its localization in PML NBs.
evidence: This is stated in the results as a conclusion from the data in Figure 7A showing that SP100 depletion increases H3.3 loading in a HIRA-dependent manner.

claim: PML NBs are membrane-less organelles also called biomolecular condensates.
source: Promyelocytic Leukemia Nuclear Bodies (PML NBs) are membrane-less organelles (MLOs), also called biomolecular condensates (Banani et al., 2017), that concentrate proteins at discrete sites within the nucleoplasm thus participating in the spatio-temporal control of biochemical reactions (Corpet et al., 2020; Hirose et al., 2022; Lallemand-Breitenbach and de Thé, 2018; Li et al., 2020).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations.

claim: PML NBs concentrate proteins at discrete sites within the nucleoplasm thus participating in the spatio-temporal control of biochemical reactions.
source: Promyelocytic Leukemia Nuclear Bodies (PML NBs) are membrane-less organelles (MLOs), also called biomolecular condensates (Banani et al., 2017), that concentrate proteins at discrete sites within the nucleoplasm thus participating in the spatio-temporal control of biochemical reactions (Corpet et al., 2020; Hirose et al., 2022; Lallemand-Breitenbach and de Thé, 2018; Li et al., 2020).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations.

claim: PML is a tumor-suppressor protein.
source: The tumor-suppressor PML protein is the primary scaffold of PML NBs and forms an outer shell, together with the SP100 nuclear antigen, surrounding an inner core of dozens of proteins that localize constitutively or transiently in PML NBs.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as a characterization of PML.

claim: PML NBs have been involved in senescence, antiviral response, transcriptional regulation, DNA damage response, and stemness.
source: PML NBs have been involved in a wide variety of biological processes such as senescence, antiviral response, transcriptional regulation, DNA damage response, or stemness suggesting that they are fully significant structures.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction describing the biological roles of PML NBs.

claim: PML NBs can serve as hotspots promoting specific biochemical reactions such as SUMOylation.
source: First, they can serve as hotspots promoting specific biochemical reactions such as SUMOylation.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as one of the three modes of action of PML NBs.

claim: PML NBs may buffer/sequestrate specific factors which could lead to their substantial depletion for the surrounding nuclear space.
source: Second, PML NBs may buffer/sequestrate specific factors which could lead to their substantial depletion for the surrounding nuclear space.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as one of the three modes of action of PML NBs.

claim: PML NBs have been found associated with both transcriptionally-active domains and heterochromatin regions such as telomeres.
source: PML NBs have been found associated with both transcriptionally-active domains (Boisvert et al., 2000; Kurihara et al., 2020; Wang et al., 2004), as well as heterochromatin regions such as telomeres suggesting an important function in chromatin domain organization and regulation of their transcriptional state (for review Delbarre and Janicki, 2021).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations.

claim: Targeted deposition of histones variants is crucial for chromatin homeostasis and the maintenance of cell identity.
source: Targeted deposition of histones variants is crucial for chromatin homeostasis and the maintenance of cell identity (Allis and Jenuwein, 2016).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citation.

claim: HIRA has been involved in intrinsic anti-viral defense via chromatinization of incoming viral genomes.
source: These latter events underscore a role of HIRA in intrinsic anti-viral defense via chromatinization of incoming viral genomes (Cohen et al., 2018; Rai et al., 2017) as well as stimulation of innate immune defenses in the case of viral infection (McFarlane et al., 2019).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations.

claim: HIRA has been involved in stimulation of innate immune defenses in the case of viral infection.
source: These latter events underscore a role of HIRA in intrinsic anti-viral defense via chromatinization of incoming viral genomes (Cohen et al., 2018; Rai et al., 2017) as well as stimulation of innate immune defenses in the case of viral infection (McFarlane et al., 2019).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citation.

claim: HIRA localizes in PML NBs in a SP100 and SIM-SUMO-dependent manner upon IFN-I treatment.
source: Mechanistically, HIRA localizes in PML NBs in a SP100 and SIM-SUMO-dependent manner upon IFN-I treatment.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a summary of the mechanistic findings.

claim: PML is required for interferon-stimulated genes (ISGs) expression.
source: In addition, we provide evidence that PML is required for interferon-stimulated genes (ISGs) expression, and that ISGs loci juxtapose to PML NBs, thus confirming a role of PML NBs as chromosomal hubs implicated in gene regulation.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by data in Figure 5—figure supplement 1C.

claim: ISGs loci juxtapose to PML NBs.
source: In addition, we provide evidence that PML is required for interferon-stimulated genes (ISGs) expression, and that ISGs loci juxtapose to PML NBs, thus confirming a role of PML NBs as chromosomal hubs implicated in gene regulation.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by immuno-FISH data in Figure 5A-B.

claim: PML NBs act as chromosomal hubs implicated in gene regulation.
source: In addition, we provide evidence that PML is required for interferon-stimulated genes (ISGs) expression, and that ISGs loci juxtapose to PML NBs, thus confirming a role of PML NBs as chromosomal hubs implicated in gene regulation.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a conclusion from the data showing ISG loci juxtaposition to PML NBs.

claim: PML/PML NBs have a dual function as buffering centers modulating the nuclear distribution of HIRA, and as chromosomal hubs regulating ISGs transcription and thus HIRA-mediated H3.3 deposition at ISGs upon inflammatory response.
source: We thus uncover a dual function for PML/PML NBs, as buffering centers modulating the nuclear distribution of HIRA, and as chromosomal hubs regulating ISGs transcription and thus HIRA-mediated H3.3 deposition at ISGs upon inflammatory response.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as the main conclusion of the study.
